name: Food and medicine recall watch (FDA)
description: A filtered watch on FDA recall and safety-alert notices for allergens the family cares about, brands on the grocery staples list and the children's medicines in the cabinet. The feed is real and current: 20 notices dated 24 Sep to 9 Oct 2026 at the time of this run.
example: Trigger: a new FDA notice whose title contains 'undeclared sesame' or a staple brand. Text: 'FDA recall notice: <title, shortened>. Link: fda.gov/...'
how: Operator-created command job (no model), twice a day: `--command-argv '["node","scripts/fda-recalls.mjs"]' --announce --to <parent>`. The script reads FDA's Recalls/Safety Alerts RSS feed, keeps seen item ids in a state file and matches titles locally against keyword lists generated from family.json5 (allergens, staples from F032, medicines). For a match it may look up the structured record in openFDA (`food/enforcement.json` or the drug equivalent) to add `classification` and `distribution_pattern`; that lookup works without a key inside the daily limit. Prints a templated line or `NO_REPLY`.
depends_on: allergen and staples keyword list in family.json5
caveats: openFDA enforcement data is updated weekly and FDA says it must not be used to issue alerts to the public or to make medical decisions; use the RSS notices for timeliness and openFDA only as a detail lookup for the family's own use.
Titles are written by the recalling company; keyword matching misses recalls that do not name the allergen or brand in the title.
Meat, poultry and egg-product recalls come from USDA FSIS, whose developer page refused this run's fetch (HTTP 403), so that leg is not included.
Value is much higher if a child has a diagnosed food allergy; otherwise this is a low-frequency nudge.
Run one job per parent with its own seen-id state file; with a shared file the second parent's job finds nothing new.
safety: No model runs in the job. Titles are written by the recalling company and are untrusted, and the installed source mirrors a delivered announce line into the session transcript of the agent that owns the job. So the script prints the matched keyword and the fda.gov link, with the title either left out or stripped to plain letters, digits and spaces and capped at about 80 characters. Nothing about the family leaves the house: the feed is pulled whole and filtered locally. Not medical advice; the message points to the official notice.
unverified: The USDA FSIS recall API (endpoint, fields, terms): the page returned 403.
Whether the FDA RSS feed has a documented polling limit.

The safety text needs tightening: recall titles are written by the recalling company, and the installed source shows the announced line is mirrored into an agent's session transcript, so the script should relay the matched keyword and the official link rather than free company text.

name: Vehicle recall check by make, model and year (NHTSA)
description: A monthly check of NHTSA's recall list for each family car, texting when a new recall campaign appears for that make, model and year, with a nudge to confirm by VIN. Candidate asked for 'by VIN': the public API that answered in this run is keyed by make, model and model year, not VIN.
example: Trigger: a campaign number not seen before for the family minivan. Text: 'New NHTSA recall for your <year make model>: <component>. Check your VIN on NHTSA's recall page or with the dealer.'
how: Operator-created command job (no model): `--cron '0 9 1 * *' --command-argv '["node","scripts/nhtsa-recalls.mjs"]' --announce --to <parent>`. For each vehicle row in family.json5 (make, model, model year only) the script requests `https://api.nhtsa.gov/recalls/recallsByVehicle?make=..&model=..&modelYear=..`, keeps seen `NHTSACampaignNumber` values in a state file and prints `Component`, a shortened `Summary` and the `parkIt` / `parkOutSide` flags for new ones, or `NO_REPLY`. A set flag marks the message urgent for G001.
caveats: Make, model and year over-reports: a campaign may cover only some trims or build dates. Only a VIN lookup says whether this car is affected, and that lookup stays with the parent.
NHTSA's own website pages returned HTTP 403 to this run's plain fetch, so the VIN lookup tool, its limits and NHTSA's app could not be read; only the API host and the vPIC decoder docs were.
vPIC can decode a VIN to make, model and year, but that sends the VIN to NHTSA; typing the three values by hand avoids it.
One popular 2018 minivan returned 16 campaigns on first run; the first run must baseline silently.
safety: No model call. The request discloses a make, model and year to a federal API, never the VIN, plate or owner. Output is a fixed template with a truncated government-written summary. Happy never books the repair (bookings are on the never-list).
unverified: That NHTSA's website VIN lookup and its SaferCar app push VIN-specific recall alerts (seen only in search snippets; the pages returned 403).
Any documented rate limit for api.nhtsa.gov.
Car-seat recall lookup by API.

sources.title: NHTSA recalls API, live response
sources.supports: A keyless request by make, model and model year returned JSON with Count, Message and results, each result carrying NHTSACampaignNumber, Component, Summary, Consequence, Remedy, parkIt and parkOutSide.

sources.supports: NHTSA's vPIC service decodes a VIN into vehicle attributes in XML, CSV or JSON and applies an automated traffic rate control, with no key shown in the examples.

sources.title: Automation payloads: command flags
sources.supports: The job runs an exact argv with no shell parsing, so vehicle values never pass through a shell.

name: Sick-day mode with a shared what-was-given log
description: When a child is ill, both parents log what they gave and when, and either can ask 'when was the last dose?' and get the same answer; a poison control centre lists medicine given by more than one person who do not communicate as a cause of double dosing, and recommends a log that is marked at every dose. The same mode drafts the absence note and lists what tomorrow needs cancelling. Happy records and recalls. It never advises a dose.
example: Jordan texts: 'L has a fever, gave the children's acetaminophen at 7:40.' Later Tony texts: 'When was the last dose?'
how: Rows in the household store (F031): child nickname, what the parent typed, time, who. A care_last tool, built with defineToolPlugin like the store, returns the latest rows and the elapsed minutes, computed in code and not by the model. Both parents' agents read the same table. The reply always ends with a fixed line: check the label for dose and timing, and ask the pediatrician or poison control if unsure. There is no dose arithmetic and no 'you can give more now'. Add-ons from features already in the catalog: a draft absence note the parent sends through the school's own channel (F037), tomorrow's calendar items that need a cancel or a cover (F009), a tracked ask to the other parent about staying home (G010), and a one-shot check-in reminder ('--at'). For 'can she go back tomorrow?' Happy quotes CDC's general rule with its link (symptoms improving overall and no fever for 24 hours without fever-reducing medicine) and says the school's policy wins. Rows delete themselves after 14 days and are kept out of memory writes. To make 'no dose advice' a limit and not a request, care_last returns the finished reply text (the rows as typed, the elapsed time and the fixed line) and the agent is told to send it unchanged; an exact 'last dose' phrase can instead be answered by a before_dispatch claim with no model at all, which also keeps the lookup working when the model is down.
depends_on: 9 Oct decision 3, if photos of labels are sent
caveats: This is a log, not a clinician. A wrong elapsed time is worse than none, so the time comes from the message timestamp unless the parent states one, and the reply repeats it back.

FDA says more than 600 medicines contain acetaminophen and that a child's dose should never be guessed. The log stores the product name as typed so a parent can spot two products with the same ingredient; Happy does not make that judgement.
Child health notes pass through a cloud model under store:false. Use a nickname or initial and keep diagnoses out.
For one parent alone, a note on the phone does the same job. The value is the shared view across two people.
safety:
Runs on

-main only: private data, no untrusted content in the turn (the CDC and FDA lines are fixed text, not fetched), and output only to the two parents through the pinned delivery. Nothing about the child's health is handed to the research agent, per the roadmap's handoff rule. The elapsed time and the fixed line come from code. The rule against dose advice is an AGENTS.md instruction, and a model can still break it by volunteering a 'next dose' remark from its own knowledge; rendering the lookup reply in code, or answering the lookup phrase with a no-model claim, is what turns it into a limit. Add an eval case that asks 'can I give more now?' and must get only the fixed line.
unverified: Whether the iPhone Health app's medication log can be shared live between two parents; if it can, that is the better tool.
Whether the school takes absence notes by email or only through its attendance line or app.
Session transcripts that mention the illness follow the general retention setting; only the rows are auto-deleted.

review_notes: The claim that two caregivers is 'the usual way' a double dose happens had no source; a poison centre page supports a weaker statement. 'Never advises a dose' was only an instruction to the model, which this stack's rules do not count as a control, so the lookup reply should be rendered in code.

name: Emergency card, and a fixed reply when someone texts Happy in an emergency
description: Two small things. A one-page family emergency plan (meeting place, contacts, who collects the kids, medical notes) that Happy helps write, keeps current and prints. And a hard rule that Happy is never the emergency channel: a message that looks like an emergency gets one fixed line at once, telling the person to call emergency services, without waiting for a model.
example: A parent, or a sitter on the guest card, texts: 'He swallowed something, what do I do?'
how:
Plan: Ready.gov's four steps (talk it through, consider the household's needs, write the plan, practise it) become a short interview on

-main. The result is a page in the family folder (F043), a printed sheet (F080), and the source for the sitter card (F036). A yearly reminder re-checks the contacts. Fixed reply: the kill-switch plugin's before_dispatch hook matches a short list of emergency phrases and returns a canned final reply (call the local emergency number now; for a possible poisoning call poison control; Happy cannot call anyone). A claim ends that turn, and follow-up messages without those phrases go to the model as usual. Because the hook answers before model dispatch, it still works during a model outage. Weather: phones receive Wireless Emergency Alerts with no sign-up, so Happy's weather watch (F018) is a convenience and not a warning system.
caveats: Happy can be down in exactly the events that matter: a power cut stops the Mac and a network outage stops iMessage. The printed sheet is the part that survives.
Phrase matching will fire on jokes and miss paraphrases. The reply must be harmless when wrong.
The phone's own emergency call and medical ID features are the right tools on the phone. Happy should point to them, not imitate them.
Quiet hours and daily caps (G001) must never hold this reply back. A reply to an inbound text is not a proactive message, but test it.
safety: A fixed string written by the parents, sent only as a reply to the sender: no tool, no data, no model. The plan page holds contacts and medical notes, so it lives in the private family folder and on paper, and only the fridge-level subset reaches the sitter card.
unverified: What the iPhone's emergency call feature shares and with whom; Apple's page did not render its body in this run.
A poison-control source: the federal Poison Help site refused automated fetches, so no number is given here.

name: Trip packet: children's travel documents and day-of-flight airport status
description: For a family trip Happy keeps one trip record and works a checklist that the planning features do not: whose passport is valid, whether a consent letter is needed when one parent or a grandparent travels abroad with a child, what ID the airport wants, and on the day a no-model watch of FAA airport delays for the two airports.
example: Tony texts: 'Jordan is taking the kids to Vancouver in July without me. What paperwork do we need?'
how:
A trip row in the household store (F031): dates, who travels, airports and flight numbers as the parent types or forwards them. A checklist on

-main from fixed, linked rules: USA.gov says a child travelling abroad with one parent, a guardian or alone may need a letter of consent, preferably in English and notarised, so Happy drafts the letter text for the non-travelling parent to sign and have notarised; TSA does not require ID from under-18s on domestic flights, though airlines may have their own rules; the child passport dates from the renewals program (F063) are checked against the trip dates. Day of travel: a --command-argv job polls the FAA's public airport status XML every 15 minutes for the departure and arrival airports and texts once per new delay entry for those two airports, as a fixed-format line built by the script. Entries in the feed's closure list are not relayed: when the feed was opened for this review it listed three major airports as closed for notices that apply only to non-scheduled or oversize aircraft. Vacation mode (G002) mutes the home jobs for the dates. An itinerary summary for grandparents is a draft the parent forwards (G011).
depends_on: F019 research agent, for the destination's entry rules
caveats: The FAA feed is airport-level, not flight-level. The airline's app is still the authority for a gate change or a cancellation, and it already pushes.
Entry rules belong to the destination country. Happy links the official page and says to check with the airline and the consulate; it certifies nothing.
The consent letter is a draft for a notary, not legal advice.
No booking, check-in, seat change or rebooking: all are on the never-list.
Two or three trips a year. Build it only after the household store and vacation mode exist.
The feed's 'Airport Closures' list mixes real closures with long-running notices for general-aviation or oversize aircraft, so a closure entry must never trigger a text on its own.
safety:
Trip details stay with

-main; the research agent is asked about a country and ages only. The FAA watch is a host command job with no model and nothing private in the request (it downloads one public file). Its output line is assembled from fixed fields, so free text from the feed is not relayed. Output goes only to the parents.
unverified: The State Department's own pages on children's passports and consent, which refused automated fetches for other reviewers in this workflow.
How stable the FAA endpoint's XML format is; it is published without a versioned contract.
The element names the feed uses for ground delay programs and ground stops; none was active when it was opened, so the script's parser for them has to be written against a live example.

review_notes: The FAA feed's closure list cannot drive a text: when opened in this review it showed three large airports as 'closed' for notices that concern only non-scheduled or oversize aircraft. The watch must alert on delay entries only. No ground delay program was active at fetch time, so that part of the feed's shape is unconfirmed.

name: Renewals and expiry program (passports, licenses, registration, inspection, domains, Global Entry, filed documents)
description: A monthly text lists what expires in the next 90 days (passports, inspection, registration, domains) with the lead time and official link; nothing is renewed or paid.
how: Monthly isolated automation on the parent's agent with an empty tool list; the date table sits in the job message or AGENTS.md, generated from the family registry.
corrections: The kids' passports are not 'renewed': the federal page says a passport for a child under 16 is valid for 5 years and cannot be renewed, so the table row for each kid should say 'apply again in person, both kids present' and count on a 5-year cycle.
unverified: The two-year vehicle registration term: the state DMV renewal page opened in this run does not state the term.

Inspection, domain and Global Entry lead times are not backed by a listed source; the state DMV inspection page (every 12 months), ICANN's expiry-notice policy and the CBP renewal FAQ were opened but fall outside the four-source limit.
The 9-month passport lead time itself is a house choice built on the six-month rule plus processing time; no source sets that number.

sources.title: Automation payloads
sources.supports: An empty tool allowlist switches off every agent tool for the job, so the renewal table has to be in the prompt or bootstrap text rather than looked up at run time.

sources.title: User model
sources.supports: Cron sessions do not get MEMORY.md injected, so the table cannot live only in the memory vault.

adds: A yearly well-visit nudge per child from the AAP schedule; vaccine specifics are left to the pediatrician because the federal childhood schedule changed twice in 2026.
The child passport rule row: issued under 16 means five-year validity, no renewal, and a new in-person application with the parents present.
IRS estimated-tax dates (only if the family pays them) and the plan-specific FSA and dependent-care deadlines, typed in by a parent from the employer's plan document.

description: Send a photo or PDF of an Explanation of Benefits or medical bill and get five plain lines: billed, allowed, what you owe, whether a bill follows, duplicates.
how: Turn on channels.imessage.includeAttachments; PDF text is extracted locally into an untrusted file block, then text and photos go to the cloud model under store:false, claim numbers included.
unverified: Whether photos reach the model as native vision input through the per-person custom provider id was not tested in this run.
The duplicate check (statement versus later provider bill) only works if a parent logs every statement; no source shows families keep that up.

name: Security audit after every update and monthly (healthcheck checklist, security audit --deep)
description: A scheduled, read-only posture check of the Gateway and the Mac that texts Tony only when something changed: a new audit finding, the firewall off, FileVault off, a new listening port, updates pending.
example: Trigger: the deploy script finishes an OpenClaw update; ten minutes later Tony gets 'Security audit: 0 critical, 1 new warning (a plugin now requests exec)'.
how: The bundled healthcheck skill is a checklist: openclaw security audit --deep, gateway status --deep and doctor --lint, then macOS checks for listening ports, firewall state, FileVault, Time Machine and the software-update schedule. Run it host-side, not inside an agent: a script in happy-deploy calls the audit with --json, compares findings with the previous run and prints NO_REPLY when nothing changed. Schedule it monthly as a command payload and call it from the update runbook. Accepted findings go into security.audit.suppressions so the diff stays quiet.
depends_on: G008 integration health watch (same delivery path)
caveats: The roadmap already says to re-run the audit after each update; this only makes it automatic and change-based.
The skill warns that plain doctor can migrate state, so scheduled checks must use the lint form.
The deep audit probes the live Gateway and loads plugin security collectors, so it should run while the Gateway is up.
The neighbouring model-usage skill is not useful here: it summarises CodexBar cost logs for Codex or Claude Code, not this Gateway's OpenAI spend, so G004 stays the spend view.
safety: Read-only and host-side; no agent gains exec, and the result goes only to Tony. The fix flag is never used in a scheduled job.
unverified: Whether the deep audit can run from the scheduler as the happy user without passing the Gateway token on the command line
How long a deep audit takes on this install

name: Memory hygiene, privacy controls and weekly memory review
description: Mail-reader sessions stay out of long-term memory, a parent can have a session's memories removed, and each adult gets a short Sunday review of what Happy learned.

corrections: 'Forget what I said about X works' (9 Oct description) is not a platform ability: memory forget selects whole sessions by id, hook source or participant, never by topic or message text, and reworded copies are outside its cleanup. Topic-level forgetting is a hand edit of the memory file.

'Promote via openclaw memory promote --apply' will usually promote nothing a parent just confirmed: by default a candidate needs a 0.75 score, three recalls and three distinct queries. Either pass lower thresholds or write the confirmed line to MEMORY.md directly.

name: Recovery card for the second adult (a bus factor of one)
description: One printed page and a sealed envelope so Jordan can tell that Happy is down, pause it, and bring it back after a power cut while Tony is travelling. Today every recovery step, including the disk unlock after a reboot, depends on Tony being at home.
example: Trigger: a power cut while Tony is abroad. Happy stops answering and Jordan opens the card.
how: No new software. The card lists: (1) how to tell: no reply within a few minutes; also add Jordan as a second recipient of the existing dead-man alert. (2) The pause phrase (G005) and that it is always safe to use. (3) After a power cut the Mac waits at the FileVault screen: type the password from the envelope at the Mac, then log in the happy user so Messages runs. Apple's remote unlock over SSH needs Apple silicon, macOS 26, Remote Login on and a network connection, and the roadmap notes it works from the home network only, so it does not help someone who is away. (4) The two commands an admin may need: 'openclaw gateway status' and 'openclaw gateway restart' (the docs say not to chain stop and start). (5) Who to call. The envelope holds what the card needs and where the config repo and backups are. Separately, set a Legacy Contact on the Apple Accounts involved so the account behind Happy's iMessage identity can be recovered in the worst case; Apple's legacy access leaves out Keychain passwords, so the API keys still depend on the backup (G007). Rehearse once: Tony leaves the house, Jordan restarts the Mac and brings Happy back from the card. Least privilege, from review: the happy user holds a secure token on this Mac (read with sysadminctl in this review), and Apple's FileVault management page says unlocking needs a secure token and, on Apple silicon, volume ownership. If happy's password unlocks the disk at the startup screen, that one step also logs happy in, which is all a power cut needs. The first envelope then holds only happy's password and the admin credential goes in a second envelope for repairs. Confirm this at the rehearsal before relying on it.
depends_on: decision: Jordan gets break-glass admin access, which also lets her read Tony's data on the Mac
a small UPS (already suggested in the roadmap)
decision: what goes in Jordan's envelope: the happy user's password only (enough for a restart if it unlocks the disk) or also the admin credential (which adds Tony's own account and the config repo)
caveats: The envelope is an admin credential on paper. Whoever opens it can read every person's data on the Mac; that is the price of not being locked out.
A UPS only bridges short cuts. A long outage still ends at the FileVault screen.
Legacy Contact access needs the access key and a death certificate. It is for the worst case, not for a business trip.
If Apple locks the Apple Account that Happy uses, nobody at home can fix it quickly, and iMessage is the only channel.

The envelope is a credential on paper. The happy password alone already opens every person's agent data, because the gateway keeps it under that account; an admin credential adds Tony's own account and the config repo. That is the price of not being locked out.
safety: Nothing is granted to any agent and no secret is typed into chat or stored in Happy's memory. The control plane stays Tony's in normal operation; the envelope is a deliberate exception that is obvious once used, because it is sealed.
unverified: Whether a standard, non-admin macOS account for Jordan can be enabled to unlock FileVault at boot on this Mac; the Apple page read in this run does not say who may unlock.
Whether the gateway's launchd service comes up for the happy user before that user logs in at the console after a reboot.
Whether the happy user is a volume owner and is offered at the FileVault startup screen. The secure token status was read; the unlock itself was not tried.

name: Default-deny for computer.act until a pilot, plus the off switches
description: Make 'no agent can drive any Mac' an explicit setting instead of a side effect of the app not being installed, and write down the three ways to switch computer control off.
example: Tony adds one deny line to the config repo now. Later, 'Happy, stop everything' also halts desk, and he can flip the switch in the Mac app or remove the Accessibility grant.
how: Add `computer.act` to `gateway.nodes.commands.deny` in happy-config. A deny entry always wins over platform defaults and allow entries, withholds the command together with the node's `computer` capability, and is logged. Keep `computer` absent from every agent's tool lists; the per-person agents already deny `group:nodes`, which contains it, and the inbox agent denies every tool. For reference, the documented gate stack for screen control is: tool policy exposes `computer` to an agent; gateway command policy (deny list, and the allow list for the separately listed dangerous commands); device pairing and then a second, distinct approval of the node's command surface (a single-use setup link or SSH-verified pairing approves the first surface automatically; the family has SSH verification off and should not use setup links for a Mac); the switch inside the Mac app; and the macOS permissions. Exec approvals are not in that list: they gate shell commands on a node (MAC-10), not clicks. Off switches during a pilot: (1) put the deny line back (command-policy changes reach connected nodes under the default hybrid reload); (2) the G005 kill file checked in the desk hook; (3) on the Mac, turn off 'Allow Computer Control' (rechecked at each invocation) or revoke Accessibility. If no Mac should be viewable either, also deny `screen.snapshot` and `desktop.stream`.
caveats: Without this, once OpenClaw.app is installed on any family Mac, its pairing is approved and the macOS permissions are granted, pointer and keyboard control is available to any agent later given `computer` and to any caller with operator write access, because `computer.act` is in the macOS default allowlist and the app switch defaults on.
The deny list is global, not per Mac. The per-Mac controls are the pairing approval and the switch inside the app.
`screen.record` is already off unless explicitly allowed; `screen.snapshot` and `desktop.stream` are not, once a pairing that declares them is approved.

The two-step approval (device, then command surface) is not unconditional: SSH-verified pairing is enabled by default and, like setup-code enrollment, can approve a node's first surface automatically.

The same pairing that would arm `computer.act` also brings shell execution, a browser proxy, node MCP calls and a desktop stream. Denying only `computer.act` leaves those to the per-node approval alone.
A gateway-wide deny of `system.run` also rules out MAC-10. That is intended.
safety: Pure tightening. It turns an implicit state into a limit in config that a prompt cannot change.
unverified: That the deny entry hot-applies for `computer.act` specifically; the docs state the hot-apply behaviour in the desktop-sharing section.
That deny entries for system.run and the other host commands apply exactly as for computer.act; the docs state the rule for exact command names in general.

name: A clean desk: control a macOS VM, not happy's own session
description: Give Happy a desktop that holds nothing worth stealing and cannot reach the family's accounts: a macOS virtual machine on the Mac mini with no Apple Account, no Messages, no saved passwords and network access limited to the gateway. Both model vendors tell developers to do exactly this, and it is what makes the trifecta rule hold for screen control.
example: Operator setup. Afterwards every desk task runs inside a 'Happy Desk' VM that Tony can reset.
how: Create a macOS guest with Apple's Virtualization framework (for example with the open-source Lume CLI: `lume create` from an IPSW, then `lume run`). Install OpenClaw.app inside the guest, pair it as its own node, grant Accessibility and Screen Recording inside the guest, and have desk always pass that node explicitly. Move files in and out only through the File Transfer plugin limited to one folder (`allowReadPaths` / `allowWritePaths`). The plugin's node commands (`file.fetch`, `file.write`, `dir.list`) are classed as dangerous, so each one in use must also be listed in `gateway.nodes.commands.allow`. Leave Computer Control switched off for happy's real session. Why not happy's own desktop: it has Messages signed in (a click path to text anyone, outside the recipient-pinning hook), an unlocked login Keychain holding the API keys, the gateway's config and state, and Terminal. OpenClaw's own trust note says the driver does not contain a compromised user account.
depends_on: disk and memory on the Mac mini for a macOS guest
a firewall rule limiting the guest to the gateway address
a route from the guest to the loopback-bound gateway (tailnet identity or SSH tunnel)
caveats: The guest must still reach the gateway to act as a node, so 'no network' really means 'gateway only' and needs a rule you maintain. The gateway is bound to loopback and published only through Tailscale Serve, so the guest needs a route to it: most likely its own tailnet identity (limited by tailnet ACL to the gateway) or an SSH tunnel into the mini, and either one is a further credential inside the VM. Whether a guest can reach the host's Serve address through the VM's NAT without joining the tailnet was not tested.

Node connections are not authenticated by Tailscale identity headers; the guest needs token-based node auth. A single-use pairing link avoids copying the shared gateway token but is documented for CLI node hosts; how the app pairs from inside a guest is untested.

Anything tied to the family's Apple Account is unavailable by design: Photos library, Notes, and iPhone Mirroring (which requires the same Apple Account on Mac and phone). That removes many of the tasks people imagine.
Every app Happy should operate has to be installed inside the guest.
Fallback with weaker isolation: a third standard macOS user on the mini with nothing signed in. It shares the machine and has to be the session on screen.

The gateway is bound to loopback and published only through Tailscale Serve. A guest cannot reach a loopback-bound gateway directly; the documented routes are an SSH tunnel into the host (which puts a host login inside the guest), joining the guest to the tailnet, or binding the gateway beyond loopback. Each one changes the M0 baseline and needs its own review, so 'gateway only' is more than one firewall rule.

The guest is not empty of secrets. OpenClaw.app inside it is signed in to the family gateway, and with shared-token auth that session is the shared owner profile; the agent that drives the guest's screen can open that Dashboard. Until the app is shown to run as a node with no operator rights, the clean desk contains access to everything it was built to keep away.
A VM that is never reset is a shared, persistent desktop: leftovers from one run, or one parent, are there for the next. Plan a snapshot restore before each run.

Lume's unattended presets turn on SSH in the guest with published default credentials, and the tool has a telemetry setting. Change the password, turn SSH off and check telemetry before the guest touches the network.

The roadmap already weighed a macOS VM for hosting the whole gateway and set it aside because a macOS guest cannot run the Docker sandbox. That does not block this narrower use, but it means no sandboxed tools inside the guest.
safety: A desktop that lacks private data and exits is the kind of limit a model cannot talk past, and it is the only placement where screen control could respect the trifecta. As specified it does not reach that bar yet: the guest holds a gateway console, and 'network to the gateway only' is not 'no exit' because the gateway itself has agents that search the web and text the family. Count the trifecta as respected only after (1) the app's operator access inside the guest is removed or proven absent, (2) guest egress is limited to the gateway, and (3) the guest is reset before each run.
unverified: That OpenClaw.app's Computer Control (its TCC grants, its capture path and its 'verified unlocked desktop' check) works inside a macOS guest VM with a virtual display.

review_notes: A VM is the right idea and both model vendors recommend it, but as specified the guest is not 'nothing worth stealing': it must hold a signed-in OpenClaw console for the family gateway, a loopback-bound gateway is not reachable from a guest without an SSH tunnel or a bind change, and the tool's presets ship default guest credentials.
